name: Ostarine

lead: Ostarine (enobosarm, MK-2866) is an oral selective androgen receptor modulator used by lifters for lean mass and a leaner look, sometimes alongside TRT or after steroid cycles. It is regarded as a milder alternative to anabolic steroids.

It binds the androgen receptor aiming for activity in muscle and bone with less effect on tissues such as the prostate. Trials for muscle wasting, including lung cancer patients, showed increased lean mass without consistent functional gains. It was never approved, though development continues for other uses.

paras: Sold online as a research chemical or gym supplement and taken orally, typically for several weeks on a lean-bulk or cut, sometimes with post-cycle support. Users report gradual lean-mass and fullness changes.

Not approved and banned in sport. Reported harms include suppression of natural testosterone, lowered HDL cholesterol, raised liver enzymes and case reports of drug-induced liver injury. Gray-market products are often mislabelled.

social.title: Ostarine, the Wonder Drug That's Plaguing Sports

chain: Lean mass gain, some fat loss
angle.text: Ostarine is a SARM used by lifters to add lean mass and look leaner, sometimes alongside TRT or after steroid cycles. It activates the androgen receptor in muscle, which supports more muscle and some fat loss. It has been trialled for muscle wasting and raised lean mass there; hormone suppression is a documented effect.

lead: Ostarine, known in the medical literature as enobosarm and by the code names GTx-024, MK-2866 and S-22, is an orally taken, nonsteroidal selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM). Developed to treat muscle wasting, it was tested in cancer cachexia, sarcopenia and other conditions, and it is not approved as a medicine for any use.[1] The name Ostarine was a tentative brand name chosen by its developer, GTx, Inc., that was never used commercially but persists as a synonym; enobosarm is the International Nonproprietary Name.[1]

In late-stage trials in people with lung cancer, enobosarm increased lean body mass but did not consistently improve physical function, and development for muscle wasting in cancer ended without approval.[1][2] Development has continued for other uses, including androgen receptor-positive breast cancer and, according to Wikipedia, preserving body composition in people taking GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide.[1][3][4]

Outside medicine, ostarine is sold online as a research chemical or gym supplement and is widely discussed on bodybuilding and looksmaxxing forums as a milder alternative to anabolic steroids. Reported adverse effects in trials include lowered HDL cholesterol and testosterone and raised liver enzymes, and case reports describe drug-induced liver injury.[1][5] A 2017 JAMA analysis of products marketed online as SARMs examined their chemical identity and labelling, reflecting concern about the composition of such products.[6] The compound is prohibited in sport and is a frequent finding in doping analysis.[7]
infobox: About 14 to 24 hours in human volunteers[1]
GTx, Inc. (licensed from University of Tennessee); Merck partnership 2007-2010; later Veru Inc.[1]
Not approved for any medical use; unlicensed supplement sales; banned in sport

paras: Enobosarm is not approved for any medical use and is not available as a licensed pharmaceutical.[1] It has been investigated for cancer-related muscle wasting, sarcopenia in older adults, androgen receptor-positive breast cancer, stress urinary incontinence in women, Duchenne muscular dystrophy and other indications; development for most of these was discontinued.[1]

Wikipedia describes enobosarm and other SARMs as sold by online vendors as designer drugs and increasingly used by the general public in gym-supplement form.[1] A JAMA paper described reports of increasing use of nonsteroidal SARMs to enhance appearance and performance.[6]

On T Nation, users describe taking it alongside testosterone replacement, as a fat-loss or recovery aid, as a milder choice than other anabolic agents, or as an aesthetic option for women, and one thread describes a user who ordered a large stack of different SARMs at once.[8][9][10][11][12] Other posters report no perceived benefit, or say they stopped because of health worries.[13][14]

In a 12-week phase II trial in healthy elderly men and postmenopausal women, GTx-024 improved total lean body mass and physical function compared with placebo.[15] In a phase II trial in people with cancer, enobosarm was reported to affect muscle wasting and physical function.[16]

Two identically designed phase III trials, POWER 1 and POWER 2, enrolled people starting first-line chemotherapy for non-small-cell lung cancer, without requiring a minimum amount of weight loss.[17][18][19] Reviews of cachexia therapy report that enobosarm and the ghrelin agonist anamorelin both completed phase III trials and both showed a significant effect on reversing skeletal muscle loss but an inconsistent effect on physical function.[2] Wikipedia likewise says lean body mass improved but muscle strength did not, and that for this reason enobosarm was not approved for muscle wasting.[1]

In breast cancer, a 2024 phase II randomised trial (Study G200802) tested enobosarm in women with androgen receptor-positive, ER-positive, HER2-negative advanced disease, and a phase II study combined it with pembrolizumab in androgen receptor-positive triple-negative breast cancer, reporting a modest clinical benefit rate of 25 percent at 16 weeks.[20][21] No trial in healthy young people using it for appearance was found among the sources reviewed.

Human research on enobosarm is extensive for a SARM, though conducted in patients and older adults rather than in people seeking cosmetic effects. Registered trials include phase III studies in non-small-cell lung cancer muscle wasting (NCT01355497, 330 participants; NCT01355484, 321 participants), a phase II cachexia study (NCT00467844, 159 participants), phase II breast cancer trials (for example NCT02463032, 136 participants), and a phase II trial in postmenopausal women with stress urinary incontinence (NCT03241342, 491 participants).[22][23][24][25][26] Some breast cancer and incontinence studies were terminated or withdrawn.[27][28]

The 2011 phase II trial in healthy elderly volunteers and the 2013 trial in cancer patients are the main published efficacy reports, supplemented by the POWER phase III design paper and later reviews.[15][16][17][2] A phase I study examined pharmacokinetic interactions with itraconazole, rifampin, probenecid, celecoxib and rosuvastatin.[29]

Wikipedia summarises clinical-trial side effects as headache, fatigue, anemia, nausea, diarrhea and back pain, with dose-related lowering of HDL cholesterol (about 17 percent at 1 mg per day and 27 percent at 3 mg per day), reductions in total testosterone in older men at 1 and 3 mg per day, lowered SHBG, and elevated liver enzymes.[1] The masculinising effects in women have largely not been evaluated.[1] Preclinical findings include a rat study in which ostarine blunted the effect of endurance training on submaximal endurance, and a cell study reporting sex-specific cytotoxicity of ostarine in cardiomyocytes.[30][31]

Trial-reported effects are described above. In addition, a published case report documented drug-induced liver injury from enobosarm taken as a supplement, and a separate case report described liver injury from the related SARM RAD-140.[5][32] Wikipedia notes that the effects and risks of the higher doses used non-medically are unknown, and that doses sold and used through online channels are often much higher than those studied in trials.[1]

A user thread on T Nation describes hormonal problems after combining a SARM with finasteride, in which the poster questioned whether the product contained a prohormone rather than the labelled ostarine.[33] The 2017 JAMA study, which examined the chemical composition and labelling of SARM products sold online, is the main published source on product identity.[6] Anti-doping literature describes methods for detecting SARMs in doping control.[7]

Enobosarm binds the androgen receptor with high affinity; Wikipedia gives a Ki of 3.8 nM in one study, about 17 percent of DHT's affinity.[1] In preclinical work it showed tissue-dependent activity, with strong agonist effects in muscle and bone and partial agonist or antagonist effects in the prostate, seminal vesicles and uterus.[1] That tissue selectivity is the basis for the SARM concept, although Wikipedia notes that the effects of SARMs in many androgen-receptor-expressing tissues remain uncharacterized.[1]

Enobosarm is orally bioavailable, reaches peak concentrations a median of one hour after dosing, and has a human elimination half-life of roughly 14 to 24 hours.[1] It is metabolised mainly by glucuronidation (UGT1A1 and UGT2B7) with minor CYP3A4 oxidation; the enzyme inducer rifampin lowered exposure, while probenecid lengthened its half-life.[1][29]

Enobosarm is a small, lipophilic arylpropionamide with a molecular weight of about 389 g/mol, derived through a series of structural modifications from the antiandrogen bicalutamide (via acetothiolutamide, andarine and the compound S-1).[1]

The first SARMs were arylpropionamides derived from bicalutamide, discovered by James T. Dalton and colleagues at the University of Tennessee and first described in a paper in 1998; the term SARM came into use by 1999.[1] Enobosarm was identified in 2004 and described in the literature in 2005. GTx, a pharmaceutical company founded in Memphis in 1997, licensed it from the University of Tennessee Research Foundation and developed it.[1]

A phase I trial had been completed by 2005, and a phase II trial was under way by 2007, the year GTx signed an exclusive license with Merck, which ended in 2010.[1] A 2011 phase II trial reported lean mass and function improvements in elderly volunteers, and the POWER phase III trials began that year.[1][15][22][23] Later, development was taken up by Veru Inc.[1]

Enobosarm has no marketing approval for any indication.[1] It is prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency, according to Grokipedia, and doping-control literature describes analytic detection of SARMs.[4][7]

subs.h: Use in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities
paras: Ostarine is the SARM most frequently named in forum posts. Posters describe it as the "least suppressive" SARM, a preference for women seeking aesthetics, an add-on to testosterone therapy, or part of multi-compound stacks.[33][12][8][11] Forum accounts also include a self-experiment tracking body weight and body-fat percentage before and after starting it, and a poster who reported a strong response but stopped because of health worries.[34][14]

Current development focuses on androgen receptor-positive breast cancer, including a phase III trial at a higher dose mentioned by Wikipedia, and on preserving lean mass during GLP-1 drug-induced weight loss.[1][3] A 2026 review of drugs to preserve lean body mass during GLP-1 therapy discusses several classes of muscle-preserving agents.[3]

lore.intro: Ostarine is discussed on bodybuilding forums such as T Nation as the entry-level or mildest SARM, often alongside testosterone or in stacks with other research compounds.[8][12][11]
